Born in Tokyo in 1997 to a Japanese mother and an American father, Inzer spent her early years in Japan before relocating to the United States in 2003.

At age fifteen, during the summer before turning sixteen, she returned to Japan alone for an eight-week trip to reconnect with her birthplace, documenting her experiences through handwritten musings, original full-color illustrations, photographs, and personal anecdotes.
The book offers a humorous and candid teenage perspective on modern Japanese culture, blending cultural observations with lighthearted reflections on rediscovering her Japanese roots.

Inzer's journey takes her through Tokyo's Harajuku district for cutting-edge fashion, the Tsukiji fish market for exceptional sushi, Kyoto in search of geisha, and various other urban and rural locations, while encountering quirky elements like high-tech toilets and maid cafés along the way.

The work combines self-deprecating humor, vivid drawings, and honest accounts of travel challenges and joys, appealing to comic enthusiasts, Japanophiles, and young adult readers interested in personal cultural exploration.
Christine Mari Inzer was born in Tokyo in 1997 to a Japanese mother and an American father.
She spent her early childhood in Japan before relocating to the United States with her family in 2003 at the age of 5.

Inzer developed a lifelong passion for drawing and graphic novels beginning in childhood, which shaped her creative pursuits as a bicultural Japanese-American. She drew inspiration from graphic novelists such as Lucy Knisley, whose travelogues influenced her approach to combining illustration and personal narrative.

At age 15, Inzer took a solo trip to Japan that inspired Diary of a Tokyo Teen; she self-published an early version of the work at age 17 before its official release by Tuttle Publishing in 2016 when she was 19.

Halfway Home: Drawing My Way Through Japan

is an illustrated travelogue that documents the solo summer journey of a 15-year-old Japanese-American girl to Japan, undertaken to reconnect with her birthplace after her family relocated to the United States when she was six years old.

Born in Tokyo in 1997 to a Japanese mother and an American father, the author, Christine Mari Inzer, returns to explore the country independently nearly a decade later, blending nostalgia for her early childhood with fresh discoveries as a teenager.

The book structures her experiences as a mix of reflective musings, anecdotes, illustrations, and photographs that capture both the excitements and occasional difficulties of solo travel across Tokyo and other regions.

Through interactions with family members and other individuals, as well as observations of contemporary Japanese culture, the narrative emphasizes the process of rediscovering personal roots while navigating the pleasures and challenges of independent exploration from a youthful viewpoint.
The overall tone remains humorous, honest, and distinctly personal, offering an accessible teenage perspective on cultural reconnection and self-discovery in modern Japan.

Inzer's two-month trip to Japan the summer before her sixteenth birthday centered on staying with her grandparents in Kashiwa, Chiba Prefecture, a suburban area outside Tokyo, where she participated in a local summer matsuri festival and shared family meals such as fresh sashimi and katsudon.

From this base, she made excursions into Tokyo, immersing herself in the vibrant Harajuku district to observe and document its cutting-edge street fashion, crossing the iconic Shibuya scramble at night (one of her favorite experiences), and visiting the Tsukiji fish market to eat what she called the best sushi of her life.
explores the author's bicultural identity as a Japanese-American who was born in Tokyo but raised primarily in the United States after moving there at age five.

Inzer describes the challenges of her mixed heritage, noting that it can be difficult to feel fully at home in either country: in Japan, people notice she is not entirely Japanese, while in America her Japanese background sometimes makes her feel different.
The trip to Japan becomes an emotional journey of reconnecting with her Japanese roots, which she previously understood only peripherally due to her American upbringing.
